```{=html}
<div class="fv-page">

  <div class="fv-hero">
    <p class="fv-eyebrow">// climate & people · history of science</p>
    <h1 class="fv-title">Pioneer Women in Climate</h1>
    <p class="fv-sub">For years I have been documenting the women who built the foundations of meteorology and climate science, and whose contributions were overlooked, delayed, or attributed to others. This is an ongoing research project, and it is still growing.</p>
    <p class="fv-sub">Text extracted and adapted from the Preface of <a href="https://aplicaciones.ciencia.gob.es/teseo/#/tesis/O628053/detalle" target="_blank" class="fv-link">my PhD dissertation</a> (2020) and from a peer-reviewed article in <a href="https://pub.ame-web.org/index.php/TyC/article/view/2779" target="_blank" class="fv-link"><em>Tiempo y Clima</em></a> (2025).</p>
  </div>

  <div class="files-grid">

    <div class="file-card" onclick="toggleFile(this)">
      <div class="file-tab">FILE Nº 001</div>
      <div class="file-front">
        <div class="file-photo"><div class="photo-placeholder">E.N.F</div></div>
        <div class="file-meta">
          <p class="file-name">EUNICE NEWTON FOOTE</p>
          <p class="file-dates">1819 – 1888 · United States</p>
          <p class="file-role">Physicist · Pioneered greenhouse effect research</p>
          <p class="file-hint">▼ open file</p>
        </div>
      </div>
      <div class="file-body">
        <p>In 1856, Foote demonstrated that CO₂ traps heat more than any other gas — the first experimental evidence of the greenhouse effect. Because she was a woman, she was not allowed to present her own work at the AAAS meeting. A man read it on her behalf.</p>
        <p>Three years later, John Tyndall published similar results and received full credit. Newton Foote's work went unrecognised for over 150 years. Today, average CO₂ levels are above 420 ppm. She predicted this would warm the Earth. She was right.</p>
        <p>She also participated in the Seneca Falls Convention, fighting for women's rights. Her paper <em>"Circumstances Affecting the Heat of the Sun's Rays"</em> was never formally published.</p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="file-card" onclick="toggleFile(this)">
      <div class="file-tab">FILE Nº 002</div>
      <div class="file-front">
        <div class="file-photo"><div class="photo-placeholder">F.M.B</div></div>
        <div class="file-meta">
          <p class="file-name">FELISA MARTÍN BRAVO</p>
          <p class="file-dates">1898 – 1979 · Spain</p>
          <p class="file-role">Meteorologist · First woman at AEMET</p>
          <p class="file-hint">▼ open file</p>
        </div>
      </div>
      <div class="file-body">
        <p>First woman to earn a PhD in physics in Spain. In 1931 she passed the national exams to enter AEMET, becoming the first Spanish female meteorologist, and the only one until 1935.</p>
        <p>She collaborated with Nobel Prize winner Charles Thomson Rees Wilson at Cambridge. The Spanish Civil War halted her career, as it did for so many women scientists. Unlike most, she was allowed to return to AEMET under the dictatorship.</p>
        <p>Between 1937 and 1940 she directed the Igeldo Meteorological Observatory. Between 1973 and 1974 she served as president of the Spanish Association of Meteorology — another first.</p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="file-card" onclick="toggleFile(this)">
      <div class="file-tab">FILE Nº 003</div>
      <div class="file-front">
        <div class="file-photo"><div class="photo-placeholder">J.E.L</div></div>
        <div class="file-meta">
          <p class="file-name">JEAN ELIZABETH LABY</p>
          <p class="file-dates">1915 – 2008 · Australia</p>
          <p class="file-role">Physicist · Atmospheric aerosols & stratosphere</p>
          <p class="file-hint">▼ open file</p>
        </div>
      </div>
      <div class="file-body">
        <p>WWII redirected her path: instead of joining the Bureau of Meteorology as planned, she was assigned to produce optical instruments for the armed forces.</p>
        <p>She worked at the University of Melbourne for over forty years. In 1959, she became the first woman to obtain a PhD in Physics in Australia. Her research covered cosmic rays, atmospheric aerosols, ozone and water vapour in the stratosphere.</p>
        <p>In 2009, one year after her death, she was inducted into the Victorian Honour Roll of Women.</p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="file-card" onclick="toggleFile(this)">
      <div class="file-tab">FILE Nº 004</div>
      <div class="file-front">
        <div class="file-photo"><div class="photo-placeholder">A.M</div></div>
        <div class="file-meta">
          <p class="file-name">ANNA MANI</p>
          <p class="file-dates">1918 – 2001 · India</p>
          <p class="file-role">Meteorologist · Ozone & weather instruments</p>
          <p class="file-hint">▼ open file</p>
        </div>
      </div>
      <div class="file-body">
        <p>Despite years of research on spectroscopy and a completed dissertation, Madras University denied her a PhD because she lacked a master's degree. Undeterred, she obtained a scholarship to Imperial College London.</p>
        <p>She made India self-sufficient in weather instruments — before her work, all instruments were imported from England. She pioneered ozone research in India long before the scientific community understood its importance.</p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="file-card" onclick="toggleFile(this)">
      <div class="file-tab">FILE Nº 005</div>
      <div class="file-front">
        <div class="file-photo"><div class="photo-placeholder">E.E.F</div></div>
        <div class="file-meta">
          <p class="file-name">EDITH ELIZABETH FARKAS</p>
          <p class="file-dates">1921 – 2000 · Hungary / New Zealand</p>
          <p class="file-role">Meteorologist · Ozone monitoring · Antarctica</p>
          <p class="file-hint">▼ open file</p>
        </div>
      </div>
      <div class="file-body">
        <p>Fled Hungary during WWII, eventually emigrating to New Zealand as a refugee in 1949. Her university qualifications were not recognised, forcing her to start over in a language she had never formally studied.</p>
        <p>She earned a Master's degree and in 1951 joined MetService, where she worked for over 35 years conducting world-leading ozone monitoring research.</p>
        <p>In 1975, she became the first woman from MetService — and one of the first women ever — to set foot in Antarctica.</p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="file-card" onclick="toggleFile(this)">
      <div class="file-tab">FILE Nº 006</div>
      <div class="file-front">
        <div class="file-photo"><div class="photo-placeholder">J.S</div></div>
        <div class="file-meta">
          <p class="file-name">JOANNE SIMPSON</p>
          <p class="file-dates">1923 – 2010 · United States</p>
          <p class="file-role">Meteorologist · First woman PhD in meteorology (US)</p>
          <p class="file-hint">▼ open file</p>
        </div>
      </div>
      <div class="file-body">
        <p><em>"Clouds are a good subject for a little girl to study."</em> — Carl Gustav Rossby, predicting Simpson would never find a job as a meteorologist if she got her PhD.</p>
        <p>In 1949 she proved him wrong, becoming the first woman in the United States to hold a PhD in Meteorology. She developed the first cloud model and co-proposed the <em>Hot Towers</em> hypothesis of tropical convection.</p>
        <p>She authored over 190 peer-reviewed articles and became Chief Scientist for Meteorology at NASA. In 2002 she received the International Meteorological Organization Prize — the first woman ever to do so.</p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="file-card" onclick="toggleFile(this)">
      <div class="file-tab">FILE Nº 007</div>
      <div class="file-front">
        <div class="file-photo"><div class="photo-placeholder">J.B.B</div></div>
        <div class="file-meta">
          <p class="file-name">JUNE BACON-BERCEY</p>
          <p class="file-dates">1928 – 2019 · United States</p>
          <p class="file-role">Meteorologist · First African-American woman in TV weather</p>
          <p class="file-hint">▼ open file</p>
        </div>
      </div>
      <div class="file-body">
        <p>First African-American woman to earn a degree in atmospheric sciences in the US (UCLA, 1954) and one of the first to deliver weather on television. <em>"I didn't want to be seen as just a pretty face."</em></p>
        <p>She became chief meteorologist and in 1972 received the AMS Seal of Approval — the first woman and first African-American to do so.</p>
        <p>In 1977 she won a TV game show and used part of her winnings to create an AGU scholarship for women studying atmospheric sciences. A legacy that outlasted her career.</p>
      </div>
    </div>

  </div>

</div>

<style>
@import url('https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Playfair+Display:ital,wght@0,400;0,700;1,400&family=DM+Sans:wght@300;400;500&display=swap');

body { background: #fafafa !important; font-family: 'DM Sans', sans-serif !important; margin: 0; padding: 0; }
h1, h2, h3 { font-family: 'Playfair Display', serif !important; color: #0A102B !important; }

.fv-page { max-width: 1000px; margin: 0 auto; padding: 0 1.5rem 5rem 1.5rem; }

.fv-hero {
  padding: 7rem 0 3rem 0;
  border-bottom: 1px solid rgba(24,37,71,0.1);
  margin-bottom: 3rem;
  max-width: 680px;
}

.fv-eyebrow {
  font-family: monospace; font-size: 0.68rem; color: #182547;
  letter-spacing: 0.14em; text-transform: uppercase; margin: 0 0 0.5rem 0;
}

.fv-title {
  font-family: 'Playfair Display', serif !important;
  font-size: clamp(2rem, 5vw, 3.rem); font-weight: 700;
  color: #0A102B !important; margin: 0 0 1.2rem 0; line-height: 1;
}

.fv-sub {
  font-family: 'DM Sans', sans-serif; font-size: 0.88rem;
  color: #666; line-height: 1.75; margin: 0 0 0.6rem 0;
}

.fv-link {
  color: #182547 !important; text-decoration: underline;
  text-decoration-color: rgba(24,37,71,0.15);
  text-underline-offset: 3px; transition: text-decoration-color 0.2s;
}
.fv-link:hover { text-decoration-color: #182547; }

/* Grid */
.files-grid {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(280px, 1fr));
  gap: 1.2rem;
}

/* Card */
.file-card {
  background: rgba(255,255,255,0.85);
  border: 1px solid rgba(24,37,71,0.1);
  border-radius: 6px;
  position: relative;
  cursor: pointer;
  box-shadow: 0 1px 6px rgba(48,56,75,0.06);
  transition: transform 0.2s ease, box-shadow 0.2s ease, border-color 0.2s;
}
.file-card:hover {
  transform: translateY(-2px);
  box-shadow: 0 6px 20px rgba(24,37,71,0.08);
  border-color: rgba(24,37,71,0.15);
}

/* Tab */
.file-tab {
  background: rgba(24,37,71,0.06);
  color: #182547;
  font-family: monospace;
  font-size: 0.6rem;
  letter-spacing: 0.14em;
  padding: 3px 10px;
  display: inline-block;
  margin: 8px 0 0 8px;
  border-radius: 2px;
  text-transform: uppercase;
}

/* Front */
.file-front { padding: 0.8rem 1.2rem 1.2rem 1.2rem; }

/* Photo placeholder */
.file-photo {
  width: 60px; height: 74px;
  background: rgba(24,37,71,0.06);
  border: 1px solid rgba(24,37,71,0.1);
  margin: 0.6rem 0 0.8rem 0;
  display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center;
  border-radius: 2px;
}
.photo-placeholder {
  font-family: monospace; font-size: 0.68rem; color: #182547; letter-spacing: 0.06em;
}

/* Meta */
.file-name {
  font-family: 'DM Sans', sans-serif; font-size: 0.8rem; font-weight: 600;
  letter-spacing: 0.04em; color: #0A102B; margin: 0 0 0.2rem 0; line-height: 1.3;
}
.file-dates { font-family: 'DM Sans', sans-serif; font-size: 0.72rem; color: #888; margin: 0 0 0.15rem 0; }
.file-role { font-family: 'DM Sans', sans-serif; font-size: 0.72rem; color: #888; font-style: italic; margin: 0 0 0.6rem 0; line-height: 1.4; }
.file-hint { font-family: monospace; font-size: 0.65rem; color: #182547; margin: 0; letter-spacing: 0.05em; }

/* Body */
.file-body {
  display: none;
  padding: 0.8rem 1.2rem 1.2rem 1.2rem;
  border-top: 1px solid rgba(24,37,71,0.08);
  animation: slideDown 0.25s ease;
}
.file-card.open .file-body { display: block; }
.file-body p {
  font-family: 'DM Sans', sans-serif; font-size: 0.83rem; line-height: 1.75;
  color: #444; margin-bottom: 0.7rem; text-align: justify;
}
.file-body p:last-child { margin-bottom: 0; }

@keyframes slideDown {
  from { opacity: 0; transform: translateY(-4px); }
  to   { opacity: 1; transform: translateY(0); }
}

@media (max-width: 600px) {
  .files-grid { grid-template-columns: 1fr; }
  .fv-hero { padding-top: 5rem; }
}
</style>

<script>
function toggleFile(card) {
  card.classList.toggle('open');
  const hint = card.querySelector('.file-hint');
  hint.textContent = card.classList.contains('open') ? '▲ close file' : '▼ open file';
}
</script>
```
